name: Uma Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm with Sunfield Energy, a firm of twelve that fits solar panels, home batteries and car chargers, and wires up heat pumps. Most days I'm on a roof by nine, then in a loft or a garage wiring the battery and the inverter, the box that turns the panels' power into what the house uses. What wears me out is ladders in the wind, and customers who change their mind about where the battery goes after it's on the wall.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools in that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I get roof layouts from customers' photos, have it draft the handover notes, and plan what goes in the van the night before. I always check its numbers against the regulations, but it saves me about an hour a day, easily.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside work, what does life look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27 and I live with my partner Tom, who's a carpenter, in a rented terrace. We've got about four months of money saved, and we're getting married in a couple of years. My grandad Walter ran a hardware shop for forty years, and that's who I want to be. I can wire anything, but the thing I really want is my name on the side of my own van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. This one is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. AI's a good tool, not a miracle, and its roof layouts still put panels in the chimney's shadow. I'd post that on the installers' forum, probably with a photo of its layout next to mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it changes nothing for me, and that's fine. Solar and batteries are busy, I've got a waiting list for Saturdays, and the tools I use already save me time. The plan stays the plan: my own firm in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Sunfield another eighteen months and keep saving towards a van; I've got about half of one put by. I'd do small battery installs under my own name on Saturdays to build up reviews. And I'd keep the AI tools, because they write the boring handover notes faster than I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit impatient, if anything. I want the next thing to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you have a waiting list on Saturdays. What's on it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly people who want a battery added to solar they already have, and a few heat pump wiring jobs. My grandad built his shop on word of mouth, and that's how I'm doing it. One happy customer on Elm Road got me three jobs on the same street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any pressure on you, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money's fine, but not loose. Starting a firm will eat most of what Tom and I have saved. If the van loan and a quiet winter landed together, that would hurt, so I'd start small and keep the Sunfield wage as long as I can.

say: I'd say AI is a **good tool**, not a miracle.
I'd post its **roof layout** next to mine on the installers' forum.
think: Nothing changes for her, and the **solar and battery** work stays busy.
Her plan stands: **her own firm** within two years.
do: Stay at **Sunfield** another eighteen months while saving for a van.
Do small **battery installs** under her own name on Saturdays.
Keep using AI for **handover notes** and van planning.
feel: **Calm**, and a little **impatient** to start her own firm.
S0.quote: AI's a good tool, not a miracle, and its roof layouts still put panels in the chimney's shadow.
fieldNote: She already uses AI **daily** but checks it, so a plateau costs her nothing.
Her drive is **ownership**, modelled on her grandad's forty-year hardware shop.
Her one pressure is **cash timing**: a van loan and a quiet winter together.

steps.text: Keep working at Sunfield for another eighteen months
Do small battery installs under her own name on Saturdays
Keep saving towards a van for her own firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best time ever to be a young electrician who uses the tools. On the forum I'd post how I quote a job in ten minutes from roof photos. Some of the older lads would hate that, and I'd get some stick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's good for me and bad for people who won't adapt. The office side of Sunfield, quoting, booking and chasing payments, I could run from my phone, and that's exactly what makes a one-van firm possible. Robots on roofs come slowly in this picture, so my hands are safe for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring my own firm forward by a year and set it up AI-first: quoting, scheduling and invoices all on software from day one, with no office staff. I'd put about half our savings into the van and testing kit. And I'd keep quoting from customers' photos with AI, so I can do the paperwork from the van between jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, honestly. A bit guilty saying that, but excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a bit guilty. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Sunfield has a lovely woman, Pat, who does the bookings, and she's one of the people this hits. I believe people should earn their own way, and I'd still feel bad if my way of earning is part of why her job went. I'd tell her to learn the software, which is easy for me to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd spend half your savings on a van. What if the firm doesn't take off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I go back to working for someone else, because installers are always hiring. Tom's in steady work as a carpenter, so we wouldn't go under. Worst case I've lost the price of a van and learned how to run a business.

say: I'd say it's the **best time** to be a young electrician who uses the tools.
I'd post how I **quote in ten minutes** from roof photos.
think: Software running the **office side** makes a one-van firm possible.
Robots come **slowly** here, so her hands-on work is safe for years.
do: Start her **own firm** a year earlier than planned.
Put about **half the savings** into a van and testing kit.
Run quoting, booking and invoices on **software** from day one.
feel: **Excited**, with some **guilt** about office staff like Pat.
S1.quote: Worst case I've lost the price of a van and learned how to run a business.
fieldNote: She sees **thinking AI** as the thing that lets a tradesperson run a firm alone.
Her **traditional values** (earn your own way) sit uneasily with Pat losing work.
Her risk feels limited because **Tom's wage** is steady and installers keep hiring.

steps.text: Put half the savings into a van and testing kit
Run quoting, booking and invoices on software with no office staff
Quote jobs from customers' roof photos with an AI tool

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt or get left behind, same as always, but I'd say it more quietly than usual. Two years is very fast, even for me. People would be scared, and I wouldn't want to sound smug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the thinking side of my firm becomes nearly free in 2028, which is great. But in 2031 a robot that can fit panels and wire a battery as well as me arrives, and I'd be 32 with a young firm and a van loan. Unless I own robots, the big installers who can buy fleets of them will undercut me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold off the van loan for now and stay at Sunfield, saving harder, aiming for six months of money instead of four. I'd use AI for everything thinking-related from 2028. The moment install robots are on sale, I'd try to lease one rather than fight it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not frozen, but my stomach drops when I think about the 2031 part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Tom? How does this land on your household?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom fits kitchens and doors, all hands-on, so we both get the same three-year breathing space and then both get hit at once. Two trade wages in one house getting hit in the same year is what frightens me. We'd put the wedding money into savings and marry at the registry office instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd lease a robot rather than fight it. Would you feel the same if it replaced someone like Pat or the older electricians?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel bad, yes. But if I don't, a big company with a hundred robots will, and then nobody local gets anything. I'd rather a small local firm owns the robot than some fund a thousand miles away.

say: I'd still say adapt or get **left behind**, but more quietly.
I'd admit **two years** is very fast, even for me.
think: The **thinking side** of her firm becomes nearly free in 2028.
In **2031** robots match her, when her firm is young and carries a van loan.
Big installers with **robot fleets** could undercut a one-van firm.
do: Hold off the **van loan** and save six months of money.
**Lease an install robot** as soon as one is on sale.
Put the **wedding money** into savings and marry at the registry office.
feel: **Anxious**, with her stomach dropping at the **2031** part.
S2.quote: I'd rather a small local firm owns the robot than some fund a thousand miles away.
fieldNote: Even the most adaptive voice turns **cautious** when the warning is only two years.
The household risk is **double**: Tom's carpentry and her work both meet robots in 2031.
Her answer is to **own the machines** locally rather than resist them.
She trades a big wedding for **cash in hand**, a real cost for her.

steps.text: Hold off the van loan and save six months of money
Lease an install robot as soon as one goes on sale
Put the wedding money into savings and marry at the registry office

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a proper head start for anyone willing to move. On the forum I'd tell people to get their own firm set up before the machines land, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to build the firm, pay off the van and have a name people trust before robots come in 2034. I'd be 35, with six years of customers behind me. Reputation is the one thing a robot can't buy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start my own firm next year as planned, van and all, and take on one apprentice by 2028. I'd move the whole office side onto AI the day AGI arrives in 2031. By 2033 I'd be pricing robots to lease, so I'm ready when they come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, mostly keen. Five years feels like a race I can win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd take on an apprentice even knowing robots come in 2034. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's how my grandad's shop worked, and how I learned. An apprentice who learns fault-finding, customer care and how to check a robot's work will still have a job. I'd be teaching the parts that last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut if the firm was slow in its first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own wage first, then the nice-to-haves like branded jackets. I'd take the odd day of subcontract work for Sunfield to cover the van payment. I wouldn't cut the apprentice.

say: I'd call five years a **proper head start** for anyone willing to move.
I'd tell people to set up their **own firm** before the machines land.
think: Five years lets her build a **trusted name** before robots arrive in 2034.
She believes **reputation** is something a robot can't buy.
do: Start her **own firm** next year and take an **apprentice** by 2028.
Move the **office side** onto AI when AGI arrives in 2031.
Take **subcontract days** at Sunfield to cover the van payment.
feel: Slightly **uneasy**, but mostly **keen**, like a race she can win.
S3.quote: Reputation is the one thing a robot can't buy.
fieldNote: The extra years turn her from **defensive** back to building.
She'd keep an **apprentice** even in a lean year, echoing her grandad's shop.
She plans to **price robots** by 2033 so they arrive as her crew.

steps.text: Start her own solar and battery firm next year with a van
Move quoting, booking and invoices onto AI when AGI arrives
Take subcontract days at Sunfield to cover the van payment

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is loads of time, so stop moaning and get learning. That's probably not what people want to hear at the pub, but it's what I'd say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years plus three, I'm 40 when robots match me, and I'd have a firm with a few vans and a name. I don't need my hands to be the thing people pay for by then. I'd be selling trust, design and sign-off, and the robots would be my crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the firm next year and grow to two vans by 2030. I'd do a short evening business course at the college, because I can wire anything but I've never done accounts. I'd keep every AI tool I use now and add the next ones as they come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. Ten years is plenty for someone who's already moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound sure. What could go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big companies could get the robots cheap and sell installs at a price no small firm can match. Or the rules could say only big certified operators can run them. That's where government should be careful, and keep it open for small firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years change your family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means we'd have the wedding we want, with Tom's family and mine, and probably kids around 30. My grandad always said build the business before the family, and ten years lets me do both in that order.

say: I'd say ten years is **loads of time** to get learning.
I'd tell people at the pub to **stop moaning**, even if they don't like it.
think: By **2039** she'd run a small firm with a few vans.
She'd sell **trust, design and sign-off**, with robots as her crew.

Take a short evening **business course** to learn accounts.
Add each new **AI tool** as it appears.
feel: **Calm**, because ten years is plenty for someone already moving.
S4.quote: I'd be selling trust, design and sign-off, and the robots would be my crew.
fieldNote: With a decade she is **fully at ease** and plans growth, not defence.
Her one fear is **big operators** being favoured by rules or cheap robots.
The longer timeline restores her **family order**: business first, then a proper wedding and kids.

steps.text: Grow her own firm to two vans by 2030
Take an evening business course at the local college

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. The robots would land when my firm is two years old and Tom's trade gets hit in the same year. What would help is rules that let small firms lease robots on fair terms, not just the big operators, and short business courses for trades people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'd want the robots. I would, if they're mine and not some faraway company's. Ownership is the whole question for people like me.

headlineQuote: I can wire anything, but the thing I really want is my name on the side of my own van.
portrait: Uma is a **27-year-old electrician** at a twelve-person solar and battery installer.
She uses **AI tools** daily and plans her **own firm** within two years.
She lives with **Tom**, a carpenter, and holds traditional values from her grandad's hardware shop.
She stays calm in slower pictures but turns **anxious** at AGI by 2028.
Her answer to robots is to **own them** locally rather than resist them.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, when her young firm and Tom's trade would be hit together.
whatWouldHelp: Rules letting **small firms lease robots** on fair terms.
